title: SRE quickplay: degraded-io-path mitigation and short-term capacity burst (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is a concise on-call playbook for first responders when we observe degraded I/O paths or partial accelerator failures that are impacting inference latency percentiles. The goal is to triage quickly, restore tail latency, and if necessary bring short-term additional capacity while minimizing work-in-progress loss.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to hosted and dedicated clusters where 1–20% of GPU capacity becomes intermittently slow or unavailable.
- Not a hardware replacement manual — hardware swap is touched on but detailed swap steps live with datacenter ops.
- Assumes runbook consumer has cluster-admin privileges and ability to launch capacity through our provisioning tooling (k8s, autoscaler, and cloud images).

When to use this playbook (triggers):
- 95th / 99th latency for inference API crosses configured SLO by >25% for >5 minutes
- Error rates (OOMs / failed kernel invocations) increase >3x baseline
- Node-level GPU metrics show sustained high NVML ECC errors, PCIe retransmits, or GPU utilization stuck at 99% for long tail requests

Quick triage checklist (first 10 minutes):
1) Verify alert and scope: query the API gateway traces and per-node token processing rates to confirm affected shards.
- dashboard: /dashboards/inference/latency-by-node
2) Identify candidate bad nodes: kubectl get pods -o wide for inference deployments, sort by node and tail latency.
3) Pull node health indicators:
- kubectl describe node <node>
- ssh (if allowed) and run: nvidia-smi -q -d ECC, nvidia-smi topo -m, dmesg | tail -n 200, lspci -vv | grep -i nvidia
- Check OS logs for I/O errors: journalctl -u kubelet -n 200, dmesg for pcie warnings
4) Confirm whether degradation is steady or intermittent (metrics over 5–15m window).

Decisions to make (decision tree):
- If node has clear ECC or PCIe errors and is repeatedly failing kernels -> isolate it (cordon + drain) and schedule hardware ops.
- If node shows high contention (GPU busy but no errors) -> consider redistributing work (scale out or migrate heavy pods) and enable per-model concurrency limits.
- If degradation is limited to certain model variants -> route traffic to compatible fallbacks and adjust routing policy in the console.

Isolation (cordon + safe drain) notes (preserve long-running KV caches):
- Use cordon first: kubectl cordon <node>
- For draining, prefer graceful eviction: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=60 --timeout=15m
- For GPU workloads that hold large KV caches, pass annotation to deployment to prefer graceful cache-save hooks. If pods do not implement save hooks, use a shorter grace-period to avoid blocking autoscaler.
- If drain stalls due to long-running inference processes, run: kubectl exec into pod, check process stacks and send SIGUSR1 to trigger checkpointing if supported by runtime.

Temporary capacity burst (fast-add) steps (cloud-backed clusters):
1) Verify autoscaler settings and any pending scale events. If autoscaler is throttled or scale-up is constrained, follow manual scale steps.
2) Launch N new instances (N should be conservative: start with number of affected nodes or 25% of cluster capacity) using the pre-baked image: provisioner start-template --image inference-gpu-2024-09 --count N --tags emergency-burst
3) Once nodes join k8s, label them for inference: kubectl label node <node> role=inference-burst
4) Adjust autoscaler or deployment resource requests so new nodes receive scheduling: temporarily increase replica count or reduce per-pod GPU request where safe.
5) Monitor tail latency and error rate. If tail latency improves, keep nodes for the stabilization window (recommended 30–120 minutes).

Rate-limiting and traffic shaping during incident:
- If immediate scale is insufficient, enable conservative rate limiting on non-critical routes and set model fallbacks in routing config to lighter variants. Use the console route override or API: PATCH /routes/{route_id}/traffic -> {"weight": {"fallback-model": 100}} for impacted routes.

Hardware indicators that mandate physical replacement and escalation to infra ops:
- Persistent NVML ECC corrected/uncorrectable > threshold (examples: uncorrectable > 5/min sustained for 10m)
- Persistent PCIe AER errors with device reset loops in dmesg
- GPU disappears and reappears from OS repeatedly (kernel module resets)
If these are present, open a CON ticket and tag datacenter-ops with logs+timestamps and node name.

Cluster-state recovery checklist (post-isolation):
1) Verify all remaining nodes have normal NVML error counts and PCIe counts within baseline.
2) Rebalance pods gradually: remove burst nodes only after load stabilizes and autoscaler can reclaim them.
3) If node removed for replacement, mark as decommissioned in inventory and attach replacement ticket ID.
4) Run a targeted load test for impacted model routes to validate percentiles before full restore.

Post-incident telemetry and RCA prompts (what to collect):
- Node-level: nvidia-smi -q dumps, dmesg timeline, kernel versions, PCIe topology
- Pod-level: per-pod token latencies, kv-cache hit/miss, model selection logs
- Control plane: autoscaler events, scheduler rejections, taint/toleration changes
Store artifacts on the incident Confluence page and attach CON and JIRA ids.

Playbook caveats and known gotchas:
- Draining a node with large KV caches can cause temporary cache-miss storms; always pair drain with routing fallback so we don’t cascade latency elsewhere.
- Some older kernels exhibit noisy PCIe reset traces that are benign — correlate with NVML and kernel oops to avoid unnecessary hardware swaps.
- Autoscaler cooldowns can hide available pods for 5–10m; when in a hurry, manual scale is faster but remember to revert settings.

Runbook TODOs (action items for improvement):
- Add scripted safe-drain helper that coordinates cache snapshots and pod checkpoint hooks (owner: Priya).
- Automate detection thresholds for ECC/PCIe to reduce human triage (owner: Diego).
- Postmortem checklist template to capture cache-loss impact on downstream services (owner: Samir).

Quick reference commands:
- kubectl get pods -o wide --sort-by=.status.startTime
- kubectl describe node <node>
- kubectl cordon <node>
- kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=60 --timeout=15m
- nvidia-smi -q -d ECC
- journalctl -u kubelet -n 200
- dmesg | grep -i -E "pci|nvrm|gpu|aer|ecc|timeout" -n

Notes to self / on-call observations (scribbles):
- During last incident (CON-3421) we over-drained and caused autoscaler thrash — need a runbook section on coordinated revert.
- Consider per-model low-latency circuit-breaker to reduce blast radius when nodes degrade.

End of draft.

Author notes: this is intentionally concise for on-call readability. Long-form procedures (hardware replacement, datacenter SOPs) live in infra-ops. Please add runbook improvements as PRs or ping owners listed above.
